newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's honourable Prince Bertil dies, aged 84.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's honourable Prince Bertil dies, aged 84.

text.p: Sweden's Prince Bertil, who died on Sunday at the age of 84, spent 33 years in the public eye without revealing his love of a British actress for fear of jeopardising the country's monarchy.
Prince Bertil, as the grand old man of Sweden's royal family, oversaw the education of the present king Carl Gustaf XVI.
The secret story of Bertil's love for the divorced actress began at a cocktail party in Punta del Este, Uruguay, in 1947.
It was there that the prince received word that his brother Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf, heir to the throne, had died in an air crash near Copenhagen.

"My older brother had passed away and his son was still very young. To safeguard the succession I had to remain a prince until Carl Gustaf had grown up," Prince Bertil said in his memoirs of the day he called one of the darkest in his life.
"It meant I couldn't marry the woman I loved. Everything fell apart."
He had met Lilian Craig during World War Two while serving as an assistant naval attache in London.

If the prince had married her, a commoner, he would have had to renounce his title. Under Sweden's complicated rules of succession, the throne could then have fallen vacant if his father had died while the crown prince's son was still a child.
The couple carried out their affair clandestinely at first, spending most of their time together at a house in Sainte Maxime on the French Riviera.
They never dared to travel together. However 1960s liberalism changed even the conservative court and Bertil and Lilian's relationship gradually slipped into the open.
Lilian bought a flat in Stockholm in 1957, where she and the prince sometimes had dinner with a small circle of friends who were sworn to secrecy.

Friends said the relationship was very warm and solid although the couple never had children. She also felt frustrated about not being able to attend glittering state occasions as Prince Bertil's wife.

Bertil often had to stand in for his father King Gustaf Adolf VI, who died in 1973. This meant performing mainly ceremonial duties as the Swedish royal family has wielded no political power since World War One.

In the mid-1960s Lilian moved to the prince's house in an elegant Stockholm suburb and knowledge of their relationship gradually spread. But their ordeal, as the prince described it, was not over until 1976, when they married.

The Swedish press kept the relationship out of the papers, out of courtesy, and it was not until the early 1970s that they started writing about it, a few years after the British press had been reporting the story.
Prince Bertil and Lilian were married at a ceremony in the Drottningholm Castle church outside Stockholm on December 7, 1976, attended by the prime minister and many other senior officials.
"I'll never forget that wonderful day. Lilian and I had been together for 33 years -- nearly half a life -- and only a handful of people had known about it," Bertil said.

Court spokeswoman Elisabeth Tarras-Wahlberg said the prince, who could have married without renouncing his title immediately after the present king acceded to the throne in 1973, postponed his wedding until the king himself was married in 1975 out of courtesy to the monarch.
Known in his youth as a flamboyant bachelor with a passion for sport, the prince during his old age indulged in the French game of boules which he introduced to Sweden.
He won several school skating championships as a boy and developed an appetite for motoring, taking part in French races during the 1930s under the name "Monsieur Adrian."
